Prior authorization is the administrative tax that specialty clinics pay on every infusion, scan, and biologic they order. Clinicore's site describes the routine in concrete terms: staff bounce between payer portals and phone calls, patients wait days for approvals, and denials arrive for documentation that was already sitting in the chart. The company frames the root cause as a gap — the staging, labs, and prior therapies a payer wants are in the clinical record, but somebody has to hand-carry them into a payer-specific portal. That gap, in Clinicore's telling, is where staff hours, patient days, and revenue disappear.

The product watches the order feed from an EHR and screens each order against payer and plan to determine whether that CPT code requires authorization at all. Orders that don't need one are marked cleared — Clinicore argues that knowing you do *not* need an authorization is worth as much as filing one, since schedulers stop holding appointments just in case. Orders that do need auth enter an assembly pipeline with urgency flags carried through from the order. A rules engine maps the payer's policy to a checklist of required evidence (diagnosis codes, staging, labs, imaging reports, prior therapies, notes), pulls each item from the chart, and assembles a payer-specific packet. Missing items are flagged to staff before submission rather than after a denial. Packets go out electronically where the payer supports it; Clinicore's own operations team handles portal and fax submission where it doesn't. Every request is tracked to a decision — submitted, pended, information requested, approved, denied — with status written back into the EHR field schedulers already check. Denials get appeals assembled from the same evidence pipeline, with the payer's own policy citation attached.

The division of labor is the distinctive bet. Rather than promising fully autonomous authorization, Clinicore splits the work explicitly: automation handles volume, humans handle judgment. A dedicated policy team maintains the rules as payers publish changes, and anything ambiguous — a new policy, conflicting requirements, an unusual clinical situation — routes to a clinical operations team for review before submission. The company says it publishes policy coverage by payer and specialty, updated monthly. The team itself reflects this blend: health-data engineers, former practice staff, and nurses who now encode payer policy.

Specialty focus is narrow on purpose. Clinicore names oncology (infusion and radiation authorizations with staging and prior-therapy evidence, including urgent-start workflows), cardiology (imaging and device authorizations with appropriate-use criteria built into checklists), rheumatology (specialty-pharmacy coordination for biologics, step-therapy documentation, and renewal tracking), and imaging (high-volume screening against payer rules). Customers run from single-site clinics to groups with 40 locations. The company reports that clinics using it submit authorizations in minutes instead of hours, achieve first-pass approval rates above 90 percent, and cut staff time on authorizations by more than half. It cites a 12-site oncology group whose backlog went from three days to same-day within two months, and an imaging network that cut authorization-related reschedules by two thirds.

Implementation is described as four to six weeks: EHR integration, payer mapping for top payers, and a side-by-side week with staff. Clinicore connects through standard EHR integration frameworks — Epic via standard interfaces with status writeback to referral/authorization fields, Cerner through standard feeds with document attachment to the encounter, and athenahealth as a marketplace-listed integration. The pitch to clinicians is that nothing changes in their workflow except that authorization status appears without anyone asking. Pricing is per provider per month with volume pricing for groups, no per-transaction fees, and no charge for appeals. The site does not disclose customer names beyond the anonymized examples.

Compliance is addressed directly: HIPAA compliance with a BAA for every customer, SOC 2 Type II certification, PHI encrypted in transit and at rest, role-based audited access, and US-only infrastructure. Founded in 2020 in Nashville by practice administrator Carmen Villalobos and engineers David Lin and Marcus Webb, Clinicore now has 60 people, remote-friendly with clinical operations concentrated in Nashville. The founding observation, as the site tells it, was Carmen's: the evidence payers wanted was already in the chart, and her staff were paid to move it through a fax machine.
